name: Wendy Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior brand marketer at a tea company, loose-leaf and tea bags, sold in supermarkets and online. I start the day with AI drafting product listings and social posts, then I check and fix them. Afternoons I do research on what flavours are trending and help plan the winter range launch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed of trying things, and I run a little online shop on the side selling tea gift boxes, about thirty orders a month. What's hard is that I'm still junior and my judgement isn't great yet, my manager Gareth often says my ideas are clever but not right for the brand. I use AI tools every single day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a bit of a let-down, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, and the people who learned them got a head start anyway. At work I'd keep showing Gareth what they can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I use AI every morning to write tea descriptions, and if that's all it ever does, I'll happily take the extra hour for my gift box shop. My job's safe, Kevin's job is safe, and we've got good savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and grow the gift box shop slowly, maybe to fifty orders a month. I'd also ask Gareth to let me sit in on brand meetings to learn judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Kevin, and how do your finances look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin's my partner, he's an accountant. We bought a flat together last year, and on top of that I've got about eight months of savings of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that tea is a crowded market. If a big brand squeezes us, juniors get squeezed too. But that's competition, and that's fair.

say: I'd say the tools are **still useful** and early learners got a **head start**.
I'd keep showing my manager what the tools can do.
think: I think the time saved goes to my **gift box shop**.
I'd feel safe with **both jobs** steady and good savings.
do: Grow the **gift box shop** to about fifty orders a month.
Ask to sit in on **brand meetings** to learn judgement.
S0.quote: I use AI every morning to write tea descriptions, and if that's all it ever does, I'll happily take the extra hour for my gift box shop.
fieldNote: She already has a **side business** and an entrepreneurial streak.
She sees **market competition** as fair, true to her outlook.
Her weak spot is **brand judgement**, not speed.

steps.text: Ask her manager to let her sit in on brand meetings
Grow the tea gift box shop to fifty orders a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's about what I expect, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work and learn, and that companies should be free to use the best tools. I'd say it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd rather be the junior who runs the AI than the junior it replaces, and I'm not shy about saying that at work. But I know Kevin's job is in the same firing line, since checking numbers is right there on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the AI tools for the whole marketing team. I'd automate the gift box shop, the listings and customer emails, so it runs without me most evenings. And I'd push Kevin to learn the new accounting tools before his firm makes him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel ready, but I'm watching Kevin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Kevin feel about being pushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's slower to change than me. He says accountants have survived every new software for fifty years. I think this one's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, which sounds harsh. Most of them are senior and good at the judgement side. If anyone goes, it's other juniors who won't use the tools.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** for people willing to work and learn.
I'd say companies should be **free** to use the best tools.
think: I think I'd rather **run the AI** than be replaced by it.
I'd worry my partner's **accounting job** is in the firing line.
do: Volunteer to run the **AI tools** for the whole team.
**Automate** the gift box shop's listings and customer emails.
feel: **Uneasy**: ready myself, but watching my partner.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the junior who runs the AI than the junior it replaces, and I'm not shy about saying that at work.
fieldNote: She expects to **stay employed** because she runs the tools.
Her unease comes from her partner's **exposed job**, not her own.
She's frank that she **doesn't worry** about colleagues who refuse tools.

steps.text: Volunteer to run the AI tools for the marketing team
Automate listings and customer emails for the gift box shop
Push her partner to learn the new accounting tools early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That one's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get to work adapting rather than asking for handouts. But I'd admit, quietly, this one's too fast for most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my partner Kevin does accounts and I write marketing copy, so in two years our household would have two jobs on the same chopping block. Both are thinking work, so robots coming three years later doesn't help either of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, no holidays, and we'd overpay nothing on the flat so we keep cash. I'd put about five thousand into the gift box shop and run it fully with AI, because owning something is the only safe spot. And we'd hold off on starting a family until we know what we're living on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Lying awake about both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the shop really safe, if AI can run any business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it isn't safe, but it's mine. If AI makes it cheap to run, I at least keep the profit instead of losing a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'hold off on a family'. How long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted to start trying next year. I'd push that back two or three years, which my mum would not be pleased about.

say: I'd urge people to **adapt** rather than ask for **handouts**.
I'd admit quietly this one is **too fast** for most.
think: I think **both our jobs** are on the same chopping block.
I'd see robots coming later as **no help** for either of us.
do: Cut **holidays** and keep cash instead of overpaying the flat.
Put about **five thousand** into the gift box shop and delay a **family**.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake about both of us.
S2.quote: My partner Kevin does accounts and I write marketing copy, so in two years our household would have two jobs on the same chopping block.
fieldNote: Both household jobs are **thinking work**, which drives her alarm.
She bets on **ownership** over employment, even knowing it isn't safe.
She'd **delay children** despite her mother's wishes.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and stop overpaying the flat to keep cash
Put five thousand into running the gift box shop with AI
Push back trying for a baby by two or three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for anyone willing to work at it, and I'd mean it. I'd post about building a small business with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is long enough to turn my little gift box shop into a real business, and I'd rather own the machine than compete with it. Kevin is the risk, his firm would cut accountants first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the shop fully in the first year and aim for two hundred orders a month. I'd keep my tea company job until about 2029, then leave and run the shop full-time. Kevin could do the shop's books until his own work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the shop doesn't grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back to a marketing job somewhere, if any exist, or something hands-on for a few years. We'd have the flat and savings, so it's a risk we can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say, good, own something. My mum would ask when we're having children.

say: I'd say there's time for anyone **willing to work**.
I'd post about building a **small business** with AI.
think: I think I can turn the **gift box shop** into a real business.
I'd see my partner's **accounting job** as the household's risk.
do: **Automate** the shop and aim for two hundred orders a month.
Leave the **tea company** around 2029 to run the shop full-time.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to turn my little gift box shop into a real business, and I'd rather own the machine than compete with it.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **side shop** into the main plan.
Her household risk centres on her partner's **firm cutting accountants**.
Savings and the **flat** make the risk feel affordable.

steps.text: Automate the gift box shop fully in the first year
Grow the shop to two hundred orders a month
Leave the tea company around 2029 to run the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a business plan, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should wait for the government to save them. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives my partner Kevin and me time to have a baby, pay down the flat and build a business before our desk jobs go. I'd still lose the marketing job at some point, but I'd choose when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the tea company for a few more years and try to get promoted. I'd grow the shop steadily with AI. Kevin and I would start trying for a baby next year, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still uneasy, if the plan's so clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point is the same for both of us, and a small shop is a thin thing to raise a child on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts. Fair rules, so small shops can use the same tools as the big ones, and lower taxes for small businesses.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty**, so nobody should wait to be saved.
I'd say it **calmly** to friends and colleagues.
think: I think ten years lets us have **a baby** and build a business.
I'd lose the **marketing job** eventually, but choose when.
do: Stay at the tea company and aim for a **promotion**.
Grow the **shop** with AI and start trying for a **baby** next year.
S4.quote: Ten years gives my partner Kevin and me time to have a baby, pay down the flat and build a business before our desk jobs go.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep **family plans** on schedule.
She still sees a small shop as a **thin base** for a child.
She wants **fair rules** and lower taxes, not handouts.

steps.text: Stay at the tea company and aim for promotion
Grow the gift box shop steadily using AI
Start trying for a baby next year as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Kevin and I would both be hit at once. What would help is fair rules and lower costs for small businesses, and cheap loans to get one going. Nobody owes me a job, but I'd like the rules to let small businesses use these tools as cheaply as the giants do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples where both people do desk jobs. We're more exposed than people think, because there's no hands-on job in the house to fall back on.

headlineQuote: Nobody owes me a job, but I'd like the rules to let small businesses use these tools as cheaply as the giants do.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **junior brand marketer** at a tea company who uses AI daily.
She runs a small **gift box shop** on the side and owns a flat with Kevin, an accountant.
She favours **free markets** and work over handouts, and sees ownership as the safe spot.
She stays calm or uneasy until **AGI by 2028**, when both household jobs are at risk.
Longer warnings turn her side shop into a **real business** plan alongside starting a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and her partner would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** and lower costs for small businesses, plus **cheap loans**.
